summary:
𝗔𝗦𝗖𝗘𝗡𝗗 is a first-person space-agency simulation built in Unity 6, where players join a Philippine aerospace design team to engineer, budget, and launch rockets and satellites. It inspires young learners, primarily ages 8–15, to see that exploring the universe is within reach through dedication and engineering. It addresses a real barrier: hands-on rocketry is costly, with starter sets at ₱1,200–3,500, mid-power at ₱7,000+, and high-power at ₱19,000+, far above DepEd’s 2026 per-learner budgets of ₱2,792 (elementary), ₱2,631 (junior high), and ₱3,264 (senior high).

Players act as mission control: receive a mission email (CanSat, Earth Watcher, or Moon Mapper), meet the Mission Director, design a rocket and payload, then launch and assess results. Three failed launches means game over; success unlocks more complex, optimized rockets. Built on NASA 3D resources and images, PhilSA’s MAYA and DIWATA series, and JAXA’s HAYABUSA series, ASCEND will be accessible to all schools, with DLC for sustainability.
details:
ASCEND is a first-person space-program game built in Unity 6. Players take the role of a Philippine space agency design team. They walk through a hangar and mission-control complex, then design, buy, get approved and launch their own rockets and satellites.

How it works:

  • AscendCAD: A computer in the mission-control room runs an in-game desktop with apps, including AscendCAD, a 3D rocket and satellite builder. Players choose from more than 170 parts based on real hardware, such as the Merlin 1D, Raptor, F-1, BE-4, CubeSats, star trackers and the Webb telescope. They snap parts together, mirror them in rings, and paint and label them.
  • Realistic checks: The builder calculates mass, thrust-to-weight, delta-v per stage, maximum payload, satellite power and battery budgets, and whether the satellite fits the fairing. Every part has a real or estimated cost, drawn from a limited government fund.
  • Launch pads and review: Players buy launch pads and a crawler-transporter, which limit rocket size and mass. They submit the design by email through PhMail, and the “Ascend Philippines review board” approves or rejects it with a checklist. An approved rocket is rolled out to the pad.
  • Launch: At the launch console, players start a T-minus countdown, ignition and liftoff with engine flames, smoke and a flickering engine light. They can switch between third-person, nose-cam and player views, and a monitor in the room shows a wide-shot and nose-cam feed.
  • Googel: An in-game search engine and parts encyclopedia with a card for each part, covering its purpose, specs, cost and history.
  • Prebuilt designs: Players can load real vehicles (Saturn V, Falcon 9, Space Shuttle) and satellites (Maya-1, Diwata-1, Diwata-2, Hayabusa, James Webb) to learn from. A trajectory calculator for low Earth, sun-synchronous, geostationary and lunar missions is planned next.

Benefits and impact: ASCEND teaches how real spacecraft work, including budgets, mass and power constraints and safety systems like flight termination. It also highlights Philippine space heritage (Diwata, Maya-1, PhilSA) to inspire local students toward space science and engineering.

Tools: Unity 6 (URP), C#, TextMeshPro, the new Input System, glTFast for importing 3D models, procedural mesh generation, ScriptableObject data assets, render-to-texture cameras, a custom in-game UI and email system, and a low-spec mode for weaker PCs. We used Unity Version Control.

Creativity: The game turns a normal desk computer into a working space-agency toolset. The player doesn’t pick from menus. They build real hardware under real constraints and get answers from an in-game review board.

Factors considered: Realistic numbers (parts are sourced from real figures and clearly marked as estimates), performance on weaker PCs, a clear interface for beginners, image sourcing and licensing for credits, and room to grow with a story mode and mission planning.
